power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Mindfulness of death (MDM) is a contemplative practice centered on death and life's finitude.
We review its concept, practice forms, and empirical findings and propose a three-dimensional framework: death-focused content, attentional regulation, and value guidance.
Death-focused content centers contemplation on death and life's finitude.
Attentional regulation maintains and redirects attention to death and may include decentering from experiences arising during practice.
Value guidance, when present, directs practitioners toward value-related understandings of death and life.
We discuss psychological processes associated with these dimensions and potential mechanisms of MDM.

We also examine its contributions to death research: introducing death reconstrual as a distinct form of death awareness, extending the paradigm from a one-time induction to repeatable practice, and broadening epistemological and ideological perspectives.
Finally, we outline directions for future research.

Building on this development, Zhou et al. (2024) further proposed the cultivation of "ideal mentalities," emphasizing that psychological states can be deliberately cultivated toward specified directions.

text.text: Accordingly, the scope of meditationintervention research has continued to broaden, and traditional contemplative practices with different objects of contemplation, training content, and psychological aims have increasingly entered theoretical and empirical research in modern psychology.
One such practice is mindfulness of death (MDM).
Mindfulness of death (MDM) is a class of meditative practices that takes death as the central object of contemplation.

It typically involves sustained or repeated contemplation of the inevitability of death, uncertainty about its timing, and the finitude of life, thereby cultivating awareness of death and life's impermanence (Moon, 2020; Shonin & Van Gordon, 2014).
text.formatted: It typically involves sustained or repeated contemplation of the inevitability of death, uncertainty about its timing, and the finitude of life, thereby cultivating awareness of death and life's impermanence <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Moon, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Shonin & Van Gordon, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Current research has focused primarily on MDM's theoretical foundations, forms of practice, and potential psychological effects.
Studies have examined its differences from other meditative or contemplative practices (Anālayo et al., 2022; DeMaranville et al., 2025; Park et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Studies have examined its differences from other meditative or contemplative practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Anālayo et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">DeMaranville et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Park et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers have also begun to discuss MDM from the perspective of the psychology of death, linking it to mortality salience, fear of death, and death acceptance (Anālayo et al., 2022; Moon, 2019).
text.formatted: Researchers have also begun to discuss MDM from the perspective of the psychology of death, linking it to mortality salience, fear of death, and death acceptance <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Anālayo et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Moon, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, research on MDM remains at an early stage, with three major gaps requiring further attention.First, training content and operational procedures vary substantially across studies; practice formats and intervention protocols have not converged on a common standard, and the key dimensions and internal structure of MDM have not been systematically organized.

Second, existing studies have focused mainly on preliminary tests of MDM outcomes, whereas mechanistic explanations remain limited and an integrative theoretical framework for how MDM operates is still lacking.

Third, although some researchers have connected MDM with the psychology of death (Moon, 2019), the relationship between MDM and death-related psychological processes-and the implications of MDM for death researchremain underdeveloped.To address these gaps, we synthesize existing concepts and findings and propose a three-dimensional framework that specifies the basic structure of MDM and provides a basis for understanding its potential mechanisms.
text.formatted: Third, although some researchers have connected MDM with the psychology of death <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Moon, 2019)</ref>, the relationship between MDM and death-related psychological processes-and the implications of MDM for death researchremain underdeveloped.To address these gaps, we synthesize existing concepts and findings and propose a three-dimensional framework that specifies the basic structure of MDM and provides a basis for understanding its potential mechanisms.

text.text: We then examine MDM's contributions to death research, with the aim of providing a basis for subsequent empirical testing and intervention development.

The core operation of MDM is repeated recollection of the inevitability of death, uncertainty about the time of death, and the brevity and fragility of life, while continuously maintaining death and the finitude of life as objects of contemplation (Bodhi, 2012; Buddhaghosa, 2011; Moon, 2019).
text.formatted: The core operation of MDM is repeated recollection of the inevitability of death, uncertainty about the time of death, and the brevity and fragility of life, while continuously maintaining death and the finitude of life as objects of contemplation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bodhi, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Buddhaghosa, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Moon, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Some MDM practices ask practitioners to repeatedly recite statements such as "death, death" or "death will occur; the life force will be interrupted," whereas more complex forms may ask practitioners to consider death-related questions, such as what they would do if death were imminent or if they could not be reborn as a human in a future life (Buddhaghosa, 2011; Moon, 2019).
text.formatted: Some MDM practices ask practitioners to repeatedly recite statements such as "death, death" or "death will occur; the life force will be interrupted," whereas more complex forms may ask practitioners to consider death-related questions, such as what they would do if death were imminent or if they could not be reborn as a human in a future life <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Buddhaghosa, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Moon, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond MDM itself, systematic Buddhist training concerning mindfulness of death may include a broader range of doctrinal themes, such as rebirth, with details and emphases varying across traditions (Buddhaghosa, 2011).
text.formatted: Beyond MDM itself, systematic Buddhist training concerning mindfulness of death may include a broader range of doctrinal themes, such as rebirth, with details and emphases varying across traditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Buddhaghosa, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Regardless of the specific form, traditional MDM aims to reduce heedlessness and attachment to life by emphasizing and reflecting on death, deepen recognition of impermanence, and encourage practitioners to value the present and practice more diligently (Bodhi, 2012; Buddhaghosa, 2011).
text.formatted: Regardless of the specific form, traditional MDM aims to reduce heedlessness and attachment to life by emphasizing and reflecting on death, deepen recognition of impermanence, and encourage practitioners to value the present and practice more diligently <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bodhi, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Buddhaghosa, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to clarify that MDM can easily be confused with another important Buddhist practice, meditation on foulness (asubha).

Meditation on foulness primarily involves contemplating the unattractive or impure nature of the body in order to reduce attachment to the body and sensual desire, and some forms of the practice may involve visualizing a corpse in various stages of decay and decomposition.
Although such practices also involve death-related content, they differ substantially from MDM in their primary aims and intended effects (Buddhaghosa, 2011; Moon, 2020).
text.formatted: Although such practices also involve death-related content, they differ substantially from MDM in their primary aims and intended effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Buddhaghosa, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Moon, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The two practices should therefore be carefully distinguished in research, application, and practice.

Modern psychology retains the core structure of MDM-actively evoking and continuously processing death awareness-while adapting the practice through secularization and standardization according to research aims and target populations.
Simpler practices may require participants to repeatedly recite statements concerning their own death while maintaining steady breathing.

More complex practices may use guided imagery in which participants visualize dying, death, or other death-related content and then consider how they should live within a finite life (Moon, 2019; Tan et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: More complex practices may use guided imagery in which participants visualize dying, death, or other death-related content and then consider how they should live within a finite life <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Moon, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Tan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to contemplative practice itself, modern MDM interventions may include structured psychoeducation on understandings of death, meaning in life, and value-based choices in everyday life.

For example, Tang et al. (2026) combined contemplative practice with content concerning the inevitability of death, life priorities, and how to engage with present life, prompting participants to distinguish trivial or unproductive concerns from what they genuinely value and to consider where to direct their attention and energy.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> combined contemplative practice with content concerning the inevitability of death, life priorities, and how to engage with present life, prompting participants to distinguish trivial or unproductive concerns from what they genuinely value and to consider where to direct their attention and energy.

text.text: Moon (2020) likewise described MDM-based death education that integrates death contemplation with topics such as definitions of death, the dying process, neardeath experiences, religious and philosophical views of death, suicide, and meaning in life.
Thus, modern MDM can range from brief repetition of death-related statements to systematic interventions integrating contemplation, death education, and values reflection.
Its content can be adapted to practitioners' age, cultural background, psychological state, and intervention goals.
Direct empirical research on MDM remains limited, with substantial variation in research design, form of practice, and training intensity.

Several studies have evaluated multi-session or structured MDM training. Moon (2016 , as cited in Moon, 2020) implemented a 13-session MDM-based death education program among Korean adolescents; after the course, students showed more positive attitudes toward life and greater death acceptance. Park et al. (2016) used quasi-experimental design to examine an MDM program lasting five nights and six days, totaling 48 hours.

text.text: Compared with the control group, the intervention group showed lower death anxiety and higher quality of life after training.
In a randomized controlled study of patients with cancer, Tan et al. (2025) found that guided MDM reduced fear of death and several indicators of distress related to death and dying.

text.text: Some participants, however, experienced discomfort with imagery involving bodily decomposition and dying or perceived conflicts between the practice and their religious beliefs.
More recently, Tang et al. (2026) conducted a three-arm randomized controlled trial comparing MDM, mindfulness meditation, and death-scenario imagery.
text.formatted: More recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> conducted a three-arm randomized controlled trial comparing MDM, mindfulness meditation, and death-scenario imagery.

text.text: Relative to mindful breathing, MDM elicited greater anxiety and fear; relative to death-scenario imagery, however, it produced lower anxiety, fear, fear of death, and death avoidance, together with greater calmness and natural acceptance of death.

Laboratory research has further compared the immediate and subsequent effects of MDM with other death-related or mindfulness practices. Tang et al. (2026) found that, relative to mindful breathing, MDM may increase state anxiety and fear and reduce calmness; relative to death-scenario imagery, however, MDM produced lower anxiety, fear, fear of death, and death avoidance, together with greater calmness and natural acceptance.
text.formatted: Laboratory research has further compared the immediate and subsequent effects of MDM with other death-related or mindfulness practices. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> found that, relative to mindful breathing, MDM may increase state anxiety and fear and reduce calmness; relative to death-scenario imagery, however, MDM produced lower anxiety, fear, fear of death, and death avoidance, together with greater calmness and natural acceptance.

text.text: Additionally, cross-sectional research provides further evidence on associations between MDM-related practice and psychological adjustment.

Among older Thai Buddhist meditation practitioners, death contemplation was associated with lower levels of depression, while more positive attitudes toward death were associated with greater well-being and gratitude and lower depression (Glushich et al., 2025). DeMaranville et al. (2025), studying adolescents in Thai boarding schools, found that MDM practice moderated the association between stress and depressive symptoms: among students who reported practicing MDM, the association between stress and depression was weaker.

(2025)</ref>, studying adolescents in Thai boarding schools, found that MDM practice moderated the association between stress and depressive symptoms: among students who reported practicing MDM, the association between stress and depression was weaker.

text.text: Qualitative research further adds practitioners' subjective experiences.

In interviews with experienced practitioners, Sadykova (2025) found that participants commonly described MDM as a practice that helped them reinterpret the relationship between life and death, clarify values, strengthen awareness of relationships, and deepen metacognition and emotion regulation.

text.text: The intensity and acceptability of the practice experience were also affected by practice frequency, practice intensity, and individual emotional readiness.

Overall, existing research has begun to examine a range of psychological outcomes of MDM, including death-related attitudes and emotions such as death anxiety, fear of death, death avoidance, and death acceptance, as well as broader outcomes such as quality of life, and values reflection (Moon, 2020; Park et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Overall, existing research has begun to examine a range of psychological outcomes of MDM, including death-related attitudes and emotions such as death anxiety, fear of death, death avoidance, and death acceptance, as well as broader outcomes such as quality of life, and values reflection <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Moon, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Park et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Tan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, the evidence remains limited, particularly with respect to rigorous randomized controlled designs.

Findings concerning death anxiety or fear, death avoidance, and death acceptance are relatively consistent across studies, whereas evidence concerning attitudes toward life and general psychological adjustment remains more inconsistent (Moon, 2020; Park et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026).

text.text: Moreover, studies differ substantially in intervention content, practice format, training dosage, and sample characteristics, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the overall effectiveness or stability of MDM effects (Moon, 2020; Tan et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Moreover, studies differ substantially in intervention content, practice format, training dosage, and sample characteristics, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the overall effectiveness or stability of MDM effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Moon, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Tan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, most research has focused on changes in death-related cognition, emotion, and attitudes, with little attention to the attentional processes inherent in MDM as a meditation practice.
Yet attentional regulation is an important process in meditation (Hasenkamp et al., 2012; MacLean et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Yet attentional regulation is an important process in meditation <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hasenkamp et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">MacLean et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, MDM practices can also contain explicit valueoriented guidance.

For example, the MDM-based death education described by Moon (2020) asks practitioners to consider how they would live if only limited time remained and links this reflection to meaning in life and life choices.
text.formatted: For example, the MDM-based death education described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Moon (2020)</ref> asks practitioners to consider how they would live if only limited time remained and links this reflection to meaning in life and life choices.

text.text: Such guidance may involve additional process variables that contribute to MDM outcomes, but its independent contribution has not yet been directly tested.
As discussed below, this feature is also present in traditional Buddhist practice and represents a distinctive aspect of MDM.

Taken together, understanding MDM merely as a means of keeping death in awareness may overlook other practice-specific processes inherent in meditation training itself that may contribute to its effects.
Although the basic concept of MDM has been provisionally defined, the practices used across studies still vary substantially.
Existing research has focused more on psychological outcomes and mediating variables than on systematically describing the structure of MDM itself.
Drawing on the specific operations of MDM and the existing empirical literature, we propose three basic dimensions: death-focused content, attentional regulation, and value guidance.
This framework can be used to describe and compare different forms of MDM, clarify how MDM may produce its effects, and provide a basis for future research and practice optimization.
First, the most obvious feature of MDM is that its content centers on death.
Specific exercises may vary by developer, training goal, and target population, but they share the feature that death or the finitude of life remains the central object of contemplation.
In this sense, MDM evokes death awareness in practitioners. Moon (2019) likewise described MDM as a tool for increasing mortality salience.
text.formatted: In this sense, MDM evokes death awareness in practitioners. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Moon (2019)</ref> likewise described MDM as a tool for increasing mortality salience.

text.text: Death awareness may also account for some effects of MDM.

Terror management theory proposes that awareness of one's inevitable death constitutes a fundamental existential threat and initiates corresponding emotional and motivational regulatory processes (Pyszczynski et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Terror management theory proposes that awareness of one's inevitable death constitutes a fundamental existential threat and initiates corresponding emotional and motivational regulatory processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pyszczynski et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Consistently, Tang et al. (2026) found that, compared with mindful breathing, a single MDM session produced greater anxiety and fear and less calmness, suggesting that death-related content itself can elicit a pronounced threat response.
text.formatted: Consistently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> found that, compared with mindful breathing, a single MDM session produced greater anxiety and fear and less calmness, suggesting that death-related content itself can elicit a pronounced threat response.

text.text: However, changes arising from death awareness are not limited to fear.

Research suggests that when individuals situate their lives within the context of death and finitude, they may also readjust their goals and values and orient more strongly toward intrinsically meaningful and growth-related goals (Cozzolino et al., 2004; Lykins et al., 2007; Vail et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Research suggests that when individuals situate their lives within the context of death and finitude, they may also readjust their goals and values and orient more strongly toward intrinsically meaningful and growth-related goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cozzolino et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lykins et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Vail et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: By repeatedly emphasizing that death is inevitable and that its timing cannot be known, MDM places current goals, relationships, and behaviors within the reference frame of a finite life, prompting individuals to reconsider what deserves their investment and what matters most. Moon (2016 , as cited in Moon, 2020) found that adolescents who participated in an MDM-based death education program showed more positive attitudes toward life and greater acceptance of death following the program.

text.text: Thus, death-focused content in MDM may not only generate threat but also provide a motivational basis for subsequent evaluations of life and changes in attitude.
Beyond death-focused content, another important dimension of MDM is attentional regulation, which is fundamental to its operation as a meditative practice.

Traditional Buddhism commonly distinguishes samatha from vipassana meditation; samatha cultivates concentration by stabilizing attention on a specific object, and death is one of the objects used in traditional meditation (Buddhaghosa, 2011).
text.formatted: Traditional Buddhism commonly distinguishes samatha from vipassana meditation; samatha cultivates concentration by stabilizing attention on a specific object, and death is one of the objects used in traditional meditation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Buddhaghosa, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: From the perspective of contemporary psychology, the basic operation of MDM resembles focused-attention meditation: attention is maintained on a selected object and redirected to that object after attentional drift (Lutz et al., 2008).
text.formatted: From the perspective of contemporary psychology, the basic operation of MDM resembles focused-attention meditation: attention is maintained on a selected object and redirected to that object after attentional drift <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lutz et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Existing MDM research has focused primarily on death-related aspects of the practice (Shonin & Van Gordon, 2014; Tan et al., 2025; DeMaranville et al., 2025), with less discussion of its specific psychological operations as a meditation practice.
text.formatted: Existing MDM research has focused primarily on death-related aspects of the practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Shonin & Van Gordon, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Tan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">DeMaranville et al., 2025)</ref>, with less discussion of its specific psychological operations as a meditation practice.

text.text: The process most often described is that practitioners establish death as the object of attention and sustain attention to it.
When attention drifts, they redirect it to death.
This resembles the cycle of "mind wanderingawareness of mind wandering-reorientation-sustained attention" described by Hasenkamp et al. (2012).
text.formatted: This resembles the cycle of "mind wanderingawareness of mind wandering-reorientation-sustained attention" described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hasenkamp et al. (2012)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond attentional maintenance and reorientation, we propose that MDM may also involve a process of decentering.

Decentering refers to a shift from immersion in one's experience to observing the experience itself-that is, noticing internal experiences without overidentifying with or automatically following them (Bernstein et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Decentering refers to a shift from immersion in one's experience to observing the experience itself-that is, noticing internal experiences without overidentifying with or automatically following them <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bernstein et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Existing descriptions of MDM practice contain similar features.

For example, DeMaranville et al. (2025) describe practitioners as keeping death in awareness while allowing reactive thoughts and feelings to pass and continuing to maintain meditative focus; Shonin and Van Gordon (2014) likewise emphasize contemplating death with equanimity and allowing experience to unfold without clinging to it.
text.formatted: For example, DeMaranville et al. <ref type="bibr">(2025)</ref> describe practitioners as keeping death in awareness while allowing reactive thoughts and feelings to pass and continuing to maintain meditative focus; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Shonin and Van Gordon (2014)</ref> likewise emphasize contemplating death with equanimity and allowing experience to unfold without clinging to it.

text.text: These descriptions suggest that MDM may involve not only sustained attention to death but also noticing internal experiences that arise during practice without becoming overly absorbed in them, followed by returning attention to death.
This pattern involves a decentering process.

Decentering may alter how death-related experiences are noticed, understood, and responded to, which could help explain the lower anxiety, fear, fear of death, and death avoidance and greater calmness and natural acceptance of death observed in MDM research (Tang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Decentering may alter how death-related experiences are noticed, understood, and responded to, which could help explain the lower anxiety, fear, fear of death, and death avoidance and greater calmness and natural acceptance of death observed in MDM research <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Tang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, existing MDM research has not directly measured attentional maintenance or decentering as process variables.
Future studies therefore need to measure these processes directly to test whether they actually occur during MDM and whether they help explain its psychological effects.
Beyond death-focused content and attentional regulation, MDM also includes an important dimension that we term value guidance.

Value guidance refers to explicit guidance within the practice that directs practitioners toward particular value-related understandings and encourages them to reconsider meaning and modify their behavior accordingly.

In traditional Buddhist practice, MDM not only encourages practitioners to recognize death and impermanence, but may also guide them to reduce heedlessness and unwholesome behavior, weaken attachment, and deepen their understanding of impermanence, suffering, and nonself (Buddhaghosa, 2011).
text.formatted: In traditional Buddhist practice, MDM not only encourages practitioners to recognize death and impermanence, but may also guide them to reduce heedlessness and unwholesome behavior, weaken attachment, and deepen their understanding of impermanence, suffering, and nonself <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Buddhaghosa, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary MDM may further provide explicit guidance concerning what is genuinely important and how one should live in the face of death and a finite life, linking death awareness to meaning in life, personal values, relationship choices, use of time, and life goals (Moon, 2020; Shonin & Van Gordon, 2014; Tang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Contemporary MDM may further provide explicit guidance concerning what is genuinely important and how one should live in the face of death and a finite life, linking death awareness to meaning in life, personal values, relationship choices, use of time, and life goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Moon, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Shonin & Van Gordon, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It should be clarified, however, that value guidance is not a necessary component of MDM.
Some basic forms primarily involve repeatedly recollecting or reciting death-related content without explicit valueoriented prompts (Buddhaghosa, 2011; Moon, 2019).
text.formatted: Some basic forms primarily involve repeatedly recollecting or reciting death-related content without explicit valueoriented prompts <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Buddhaghosa, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Moon, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Value guidance is therefore better understood as an important but variable dimension of MDM practice.

From a broader theoretical perspective, value-oriented practices may influence cognitive and affective responses by changing how individuals interpret their experiences. Dahl et al. (2015) classified death contemplation as a value-oriented constructive practice and proposed that such practices may operate through processes such as cognitive reappraisal.
text.formatted: From a broader theoretical perspective, value-oriented practices may influence cognitive and affective responses by changing how individuals interpret their experiences. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dahl et al. (2015)</ref> classified death contemplation as a value-oriented constructive practice and proposed that such practices may operate through processes such as cognitive reappraisal.

text.text: More broadly, research on values has shown that reflection on personally important values can facilitate information acceptance and changes in intentions and behavior (Epton et al., 2015).
text.formatted: More broadly, research on values has shown that reflection on personally important values can facilitate information acceptance and changes in intentions and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Epton et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Existing MDM research also provides some indirect evidence that value guidance may contribute to practice outcomes. Tang et al. (2026) found that, compared with death-scenario imagination, MDM reduced anxiety, fear, fear of death, and death avoidance while increasing calmness and natural acceptance of death.
text.formatted: Existing MDM research also provides some indirect evidence that value guidance may contribute to practice outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> found that, compared with death-scenario imagination, MDM reduced anxiety, fear, fear of death, and death avoidance while increasing calmness and natural acceptance of death.

text.text: These findings suggest that the effects of MDM may not arise from death-related content alone and that additional guidance within the practice may also contribute.
However, the study could not determine whether these differences were specifically attributable to value guidance or distinguish its contribution from those of other practice dimensions.

At the same time, death awareness itself may prompt values reflection and changes in attitudes toward life (Cozzolino et al., 2004; Lykins et al., 2007), making it difficult to determine how much of the observed effects can be independently attributed to value guidance.
text.formatted: At the same time, death awareness itself may prompt values reflection and changes in attitudes toward life <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cozzolino et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lykins et al., 2007)</ref>, making it difficult to determine how much of the observed effects can be independently attributed to value guidance.

text.text: Overall, existing evidence provides theoretical and indirect support for a possible role of value guidance, but its independent contribution has not yet been directly tested and should be examined through targeted comparative designs.
In addition, whereas death-focused content is relatively consistent across MDM practices, value guidance varies considerably.

For example, Moon's (2020) intervention emphasizes meaning in life and valuing one's limited lifetime, whereas the intervention described by Tang et al. (2026) places greater emphasis on life priorities and self-regulation.
text.formatted: For example, Moon's (2020) intervention emphasizes meaning in life and valuing one's limited lifetime, whereas the intervention described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> places greater emphasis on life priorities and self-regulation.

text.text: Which forms of guidance are effective, and whether different forms produce distinct outcomes, remain open questions.
Overall, value guidance should be treated as an important practice dimension that can shape MDM outcomes rather than being reduced to death-focused content alone.
As discussed below, this dimension also provides an important basis for understanding MDM's distinctive contribution to death research.
Beyond functioning as a meditation technique, MDM also offers death research a distinctive form of death awareness.
Previous research on death awareness has focused primarily on death anxiety and death reflection.

Research on death anxiety examines responses such as anxiety, avoidance, and defensiveness when individuals confront death, whereas death reflection uses specific death scenarios, life review, and questions about relationships and values to prompt consideration of what death means for one's own life (Greenberg et al., 1990; Pyszczynski et al., 1999; Blackie et al., 2016; Cozzolino et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Research on death anxiety examines responses such as anxiety, avoidance, and defensiveness when individuals confront death, whereas death reflection uses specific death scenarios, life review, and questions about relationships and values to prompt consideration of what death means for one's own life <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Greenberg et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Pyszczynski et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Blackie et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cozzolino et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: As discussed above, MDM can likewise be understood as a form of death awareness (Moon, 2019), but the form it produces differs from these two.
text.formatted: As discussed above, MDM can likewise be understood as a form of death awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Moon, 2019)</ref>, but the form it produces differs from these two.

text.text: We refer to this form as death reconstrual: death awareness that emerges as individuals sustain attention to death and their related psychological responses while reprocessing and reorganizing their understanding of death and its relationship to life.
Such death reconstrual differs from existing forms of death awareness in several ways (Table 1).
text.formatted: Such death reconstrual differs from existing forms of death awareness in several ways (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: First, death reconstrual differs from existing forms of death awareness in how deathrelated content is processed, a difference that arises from MDM as a practice.

Prior research has characterized death anxiety as an affective "hot" response in which confrontation with mortality elicits relatively direct and intense emotional reactions, whereas death reflection is more cognitive and "cool," involving deliberate consideration of death and its meaning for life (Grant & Wade-Benzoni, 2009; Yuan et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Prior research has characterized death anxiety as an affective "hot" response in which confrontation with mortality elicits relatively direct and intense emotional reactions, whereas death reflection is more cognitive and "cool," involving deliberate consideration of death and its meaning for life <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Grant & Wade-Benzoni, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Yuan et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Death reconstrual, by contrast, involves a more integrative mode of processing that includes both emotional experience and cognitive reflection.
It also incorporates decentering: individuals not only experience death-related thoughts and emotions but also notice their current psychological states and changes in those states.

Death anxiety and death reflection primarily concern the emotional or cognitive responses elicited by death-related situations and do not, in themselves, emphasize further monitoring of those responses.
Second, death reconstrual differs from existing forms of death awareness in whether death is continuously maintained as the object of attention.

Death anxiety and death reflection are typically elicited by death-related stimuli or scenarios, in which death-related content primarily serves as a cue for subsequent emotional responses, cognitive processing, or reflection on meaning; these downstream processes may persist even when death itself is no longer in focal attention (Pyszczynski et al., 1999; Grant & Wade-Benzoni, 2009; Burke et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Death anxiety and death reflection are typically elicited by death-related stimuli or scenarios, in which death-related content primarily serves as a cue for subsequent emotional responses, cognitive processing, or reflection on meaning; these downstream processes may persist even when death itself is no longer in focal attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pyszczynski et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Grant & Wade-Benzoni, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Burke et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, in death reconstrual, death is not merely the starting point for subsequent responses but remains an object to which attention is repeatedly maintained and returned throughout the practice.
When attention drifts, practitioners redirect it to death, making death awareness itself a process sustained through continued practice.
Third, death reconstrual differs from existing forms of death awareness in the source and controllability of its content.
In death anxiety, specific associations, emotions, and defensive responses arise largely spontaneously.

Death reflection constrains the scope of reflection through particular scenarios and questions, but the specific content and meaning ultimately generated still arise primarily from the individual (Blackie et al., 2016; Cozzolino et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Death reflection constrains the scope of reflection through particular scenarios and questions, but the specific content and meaning ultimately generated still arise primarily from the individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blackie et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cozzolino et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: MDM, by contrast, organizes death-related processing through predetermined contemplative themes and guidance, enabling practitioners to engage with death in relatively specified ways.
Intervention developers can therefore design the presentation and sequence of death-related content more explicitly.
They cannot determine the understanding practitioners ultimately develop, but the processing context is more amenable to intervention design.
Fourth, death reconstrual also differs from existing forms of death awareness in terms of systematicity.
Here, systematicity primarily refers to the extent to which the content of death awareness is organized according to a certain sequence and structure to form an integrated whole.
Death anxiety mainly consists of emotional and defensive responses elicited by deathrelated stimuli.
Its content is relatively fragmented and therefore exhibits a relatively low degree of systematicity (Greenberg et al., 1990; Pyszczynski et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Its content is relatively fragmented and therefore exhibits a relatively low degree of systematicity <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Greenberg et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Pyszczynski et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Death reflection, by contrast, exhibits a certain degree of systematicity.

After presenting a death-related scenario, researchers typically use a series of interrelated questions to guide individuals' reflection, thereby giving their thinking a certain organizational structure (Cozzolino et al., 2004; Blackie et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2019).
text.formatted: After presenting a death-related scenario, researchers typically use a series of interrelated questions to guide individuals' reflection, thereby giving their thinking a certain organizational structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cozzolino et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Blackie et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Yuan et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Death reconstrual is more systematic because the MDM on which it is based is itself organized in a relatively systematic manner.

For example, the MDM developed by Tang et al. (2026) presents its practice procedures, core content, and value-oriented guidance to practitioners in a particular sequence, with these components being interconnected and building upon one another to form an organized whole.
text.formatted: For example, the MDM developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> presents its practice procedures, core content, and value-oriented guidance to practitioners in a particular sequence, with these components being interconnected and building upon one another to form an organized whole.

text.text: Rather than functioning as isolated exercises, the different components are arranged so that earlier practices provide a basis for subsequent reflection, reinterpretation, and value-oriented consideration.
Thus, compared with death anxiety and death reflection, death reconstrual exhibits a higher degree of systematicity
MDM also provides a new practice paradigm for studying death awareness.

Research on death anxiety and death reflection has primarily used one-time death stimuli, scenarios, or reflective tasks and then examined psychological and behavioral outcomes after death awareness was induced (Greenberg et al., 1990; Cozzolino et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Research on death anxiety and death reflection has primarily used one-time death stimuli, scenarios, or reflective tasks and then examined psychological and behavioral outcomes after death awareness was induced <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Greenberg et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cozzolino et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: MDM can likewise be used in single-session experiments, but a more important contribution is that it can be developed into repeated practice lasting days or weeks (Park et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: MDM can likewise be used in single-session experiments, but a more important contribution is that it can be developed into repeated practice lasting days or weeks <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Park et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Death awareness thus need not remain a state briefly induced in a single experiment; it can become a process that recurs and changes over a longer period.
Such prolonged and repeated practice allows researchers to observe the unfolding process of death awareness rather than merely measuring outcomes after a single induction.
Researchers can track how death-related cognitions, emotions, and attitudes change as individuals repeatedly confront death.
Death research can therefore expand from asking primarily "what outcomes does death awareness produce?"
to examining "how does death awareness unfold and change?"
Shortterm states of death awareness and longer-term changes in attitudes toward death can be studied within the same practice process.
Compared with one-time experiments, this approach creates new conditions for understanding the dynamic process and longer-term development of death awareness.

It is worth noting that death-education programs lasting several weeks already exist, but these studies generally organize death-related content through courses and didactic activities (Testoni et al., 2021).
text.formatted: It is worth noting that death-education programs lasting several weeks already exist, but these studies generally organize death-related content through courses and didactic activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Testoni et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: MDM differs in that its core is the repeated performance of death-related psychological exercises, through which individuals repeatedly enter and process death awareness.

MDM therefore extends death research not simply by lengthening the duration of an intervention but by transforming death awareness from a one-time experimental state into an object of inquiry that can be repeatedly practiced, tracked over time, and examined as it changes.
It thus offers a research paradigm centered on sustained practice and repeated training.

Finally, the nature of MDM practice may also shape the epistemological and ideological stance of the research in which it is used. Tang et al. (2026) emphasized that their MDM practice drew on Buddhist traditions while also being inspired by ideal psychology.
text.formatted: Finally, the nature of MDM practice may also shape the epistemological and ideological stance of the research in which it is used. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tang et al. (2026)</ref> emphasized that their MDM practice drew on Buddhist traditions while also being inspired by ideal psychology.

text.text: Ideal psychology is a psychological approach that emphasizes future-oriented perspectives.

Its ideological orientation includes exploring new possibilities, critically examining the present and the everyday, and using professional methods to move beyond ordinary psychological functioning; epistemologically, it is closer to critical theory than to logical positivism (Zeng, 2025).
text.formatted: Its ideological orientation includes exploring new possibilities, critically examining the present and the everyday, and using professional methods to move beyond ordinary psychological functioning; epistemologically, it is closer to critical theory than to logical positivism <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Zeng, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Through intensive and repeated practice, MDM cultivates deliberately designed responses to death, reflecting ideal psychology's emphasis on using professional training to move beyond everyday psychological reactions.

In particular, MDM entails redesigning responses to death that are often treated as instinctive: the practice does not merely observe fear, rejection, and avoidance as they arise naturally but attempts to alter these responses through training.

This feature reflects ideal psychology's orientation toward critically examining and moving beyond existing reality and its assumption that psychological responses remain open to further change (Tang et al., 2026; Zeng, 2025).
text.formatted: This feature reflects ideal psychology's orientation toward critically examining and moving beyond existing reality and its assumption that psychological responses remain open to further change <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Tang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Zeng, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, previous death research has more often adopted a logical-positivist approach aimed at identifying psychological regularities that already exist when people confront death.

Terror management theory, for example, proposes that death awareness elicits proximal and distal defenses and treats these responses as relatively entrenched psychological mechanisms in the face of mortality threat (Pyszczynski et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Terror management theory, for example, proposes that death awareness elicits proximal and distal defenses and treats these responses as relatively entrenched psychological mechanisms in the face of mortality threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Pyszczynski et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: This research tradition primarily asks, "How do people respond when they confront death?"
MDM shifts the question toward, "Can these responses be changed through training?"
The two approaches therefore differ not only in the death-related responses they examine but also in their research paradigms.
This does not mean that all research on MDM must adopt a critical ideological or epistemological stance.
Researchers can treat MDM as an established traditional practice and study its effects and mechanisms within a logical-positivist framework.
Nevertheless, MDM as a practice inherently contains an intention to modify responses to death through training.
In this respect, it differs from research that primarily describes death anxiety or guides death reflection.

Note.
The dimensions synthesize the distinctions developed in the preceding text; death reconstrual is proposed here as a theoretical construct.
Existing research provides preliminary evidence of potentially beneficial effects of MDM, and several directions warrant future study.
First, future research should further test MDM's effects and broaden the range of outcome variables.
The empirical literature remains limited, and existing findings require replication across samples and contexts.
The present analysis also suggests that some outcomes potentially associated with the three dimensions of MDM remain largely unexamined, particularly attention-related outcomes.

This article reviews the concept, practice forms, and existing research on mindfulness of death (MDM) and proposes a three-dimensional framework of death-focused content, attentional regulation, and value guidance for understanding its structure and potential mechanisms.

It further situates MDM within death research by introducing death reconstrual as a distinctive form of death awareness, highlighting a practice paradigm in which death awareness can be repeatedly trained and observed over time, and considering its broader epistemological and ideological implications.
Together, these contributions provide a theoretical basis for the empirical study, refinement, and application of MDM.

Compared with first-generation mindfulness-based interventions, second-generation approaches further incorporate ethics, compassion, and traditional contemplative themes such as impermanence and emptiness/nonself empirical testing in contemporary MDM research.
Second, research should identify the active dimensions of MDM.
As proposed above, MDM practices can combine several intertwined practice dimensions, and it remains unclear which effects are attributable to each dimension or whether the dimensions interact.

The present article provides a three-dimensional framework and analyzes these dimensions conceptually, but empirical methods such as component dismantling and targeted experimental manipulation are needed to determine the sources of observed effects.
This work would help establish whether MDM has mechanisms distinctive from other meditation or death-related practices and provide a basis for optimizing training.
Third, research should clarify boundary conditions and optimize practice design.
MDM is content-rich and flexible, and different goals and populations may require different emphases.
